newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile's Frei to talk trade, politics on U.S. trip.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Frei to talk trade, politics on U.S. trip.

text.p: Chilean President Eduardo Frei will discuss hemispheric policies and Chile's long-awaited entry to NAFTA during his official visit to the United States this month, said Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza on Monday.
"In terms of politics, the most important (issues) will be an evaluation of democracy, peace and security in the hemisphere," Insulza told reporters after meeting White House aide Thomas McLarty.
McLarty arrived in Santiago on Sunday hold talks with Chilean officials about Frei's meeting with President Bill Clinton on February 26.
Frei's four-day visit will be the first official trip by a Latin American leader to the United States since Clinton's inauguration in his second term of office last month.
The two leaders will discuss Chile's role in peacekeeping operations, its membership of the U.N. Security Council and the next Americas Summit which will take place in Santiago in 1998.
Chile is also hoping for progress on its much-delayed entry into NAFTA which was stalled last year due to internal political difficulties in Washington, said Insulza.
"I imagine that they will inform us of progress made with "fast-track" and we will evaluate the real possibilities of reaching agreement (on fast track)," he said.
Chile was invited to join the trade bloc, which links the United States, Canada and Mexico, at the Americas Summit in Miami in December 1994.

But its hopes were dashed when talks over "fast-track" legislation died in Congress last year. The invitation was given fresh impetus last week when Republican Congressional leaders supported the idea of approving the legislation for trade agreements.
"Fast track" gives U.S. negotiators power to negotiate trade accords which Congress must either accept or reject, without the power to make changes.

Chilean officials have refused to negotiate unless U.S. representatives have this authority, as they fear that without it, Congress would unpick any accord under pressure from special interest groups.
Wary of fresh delays, government has reacted cautiously news of support from Republican leaders for extending NAFTA to Chile.
"We are interested in a trade agreement with the United States, but at the same time we do not believe we are in a situation of urgency to put on excessive pressure," said Insulza.
